subject: chemistry
title: Electron configuration
summary: How electrons are arranged in shells for the first 20 elements, what valence electrons are, and how they link to an element's group and reactivity.
body:
The way electrons are arranged around the nucleus decides how an atom behaves. It explains why sodium explodes in water while neon does nothing at all, and why elements in the same column of the periodic table act alike. Learning to write electron configurations is one of the most useful skills in Year 10 Chemistry.

## Think of it like this

### Shells are like filling seats on a bus

Imagine a bus where people always fill the seats nearest the door first. **Shell 1** is the front row with only 2 seats, the next section has 8, then another 8, and then the back section starts filling. Electrons fill the **lowest-energy** shell first, just like passengers taking the closest seat, and only move further back when the front is full. So potassium's 19 electrons sit as **2, 8, 8, 1** – one passenger has had to start the back section.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* passengers choose seats, but electrons simply settle into the most stable (lowest-energy) arrangement, and in VCE you'll learn the "sections" are really subshells with more detailed rules.

### Valence electrons are like the players on the boundary line

In a footy match, it's the players on the outside of a pack who actually touch the other team first. **Valence electrons** are the electrons in the **valence shell** – the outermost one – so they're the ones that meet other atoms and take part in reactions. The inner electrons are buried in the middle of the pack and don't get involved. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they "play" the same way and have **similar chemical properties**.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* inner electrons aren't completely irrelevant – they shield the outer electrons from the nucleus, which affects how tightly the valence electrons are held.

### Reaching a full outer shell is like rounding up to a full carton of eggs

A carton holds 8 (for this analogy). If you have 1 egg, it's easiest to give it away; if you have 7, it's easiest to grab one more. Atoms do the same thing to reach a full outer shell like a **noble gas** – the **octet rule**. Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses its 1 outer electron to become Na⁺ (2, 8), and chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains 1 to become Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8). The fewer electrons an atom has to move, the more reactive it is.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* atoms don't "want" anything – losing or gaining electrons happens because the resulting arrangement is lower in energy, and some atoms share electrons instead of swapping them.

### In real life

The bright colours in fireworks come from electrons in metal atoms jumping to higher shells and dropping back down, giving off light. Neon signs glow for the same reason, while the full outer shell of argon is why it's used to fill some light globes – it doesn't react with the hot filament.

## Key ideas

### Electron shells

Electrons do not move randomly around the nucleus. They are found in **shells**, also called **energy levels**. Shells are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 going outwards from the nucleus.

- Shell 1 is closest to the nucleus and has the **lowest energy**.
- Electrons in shells further out have more energy and are held less tightly, because they are further from the positive nucleus.

Electrons fill the lowest-energy shell first, because that is the most stable arrangement. When one shell is full, electrons start filling the next one.

### How many electrons fit in each shell

For the first 20 elements we use a simple rule:

| Shell | Maximum electrons (first 20 elements) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 8 |
| 3 | 8 |
| 4 | 2 (for potassium and calcium) |

This is the **2, 8, 8, 2 model**. (Shell 3 can actually hold up to 18 electrons, but for elements up to calcium the fourth shell starts filling after shell 3 holds 8. You will learn why in VCE using subshells.)

### Writing an electron configuration

An **electron configuration** lists the number of electrons in each shell, starting from shell 1, separated by commas. To write one:

1. Find the atomic number – this equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
2. Fill shell 1 (up to 2), then shell 2 (up to 8), then shell 3 (up to 8), then shell 4.

The first 20 elements:

| Element | Z | Configuration | Element | Z | Configuration |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H | 1 | 1 | Na | 11 | 2, 8, 1 |
| He | 2 | 2 | Mg | 12 | 2, 8, 2 |
| Li | 3 | 2, 1 | Al | 13 | 2, 8, 3 |
| Be | 4 | 2, 2 | Si | 14 | 2, 8, 4 |
| B | 5 | 2, 3 | P | 15 | 2, 8, 5 |
| C | 6 | 2, 4 | S | 16 | 2, 8, 6 |
| N | 7 | 2, 5 | Cl | 17 | 2, 8, 7 |
| O | 8 | 2, 6 | Ar | 18 | 2, 8, 8 |
| F | 9 | 2, 7 | K | 19 | 2, 8, 8, 1 |
| Ne | 10 | 2, 8 | Ca | 20 | 2, 8, 8, 2 |

You can also draw a **shell diagram** (Bohr diagram): the symbol in the middle with circles around it for each shell, and dots or crosses on the circles for the electrons.

### Valence electrons

The **valence shell** is the outermost shell that contains electrons. The electrons in it are called **valence electrons**. These are the electrons that take part in chemical reactions, because they are on the outside of the atom where they can meet other atoms.

For example, chlorine (2, 8, 7) has 7 valence electrons, and calcium (2, 8, 8, 2) has 2.

### Links to the periodic table

Electron configuration explains the layout of the periodic table:

- The **period** (row) number equals the **number of occupied shells**. Sodium (2, 8, 1) uses three shells, so it is in period 3.
- For the main groups, the number of valence electrons matches the group. Group 1 elements have 1 valence electron, group 2 have 2, and groups 13 to 18 have 3 to 8 (just subtract 10). Helium is the exception: it is in group 18 but has only 2 electrons, which fill its only shell.

Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, which is why they have **similar chemical properties**.

### Stability and reactivity

The **noble gases** (group 18) have full outer shells (helium 2, neon 2, 8, argon 2, 8, 8). A full outer shell is very stable, so noble gases hardly react at all.

Other atoms react in ways that give them a full outer shell like a noble gas – this idea is often called the **octet rule**, because for most atoms a full outer shell means 8 electrons.

- Atoms with only 1, 2 or 3 valence electrons (metals) tend to **lose** them to form positive ions. Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses 1 electron to become Na⁺ (2, 8).
- Atoms with 5, 6 or 7 valence electrons (non-metals) tend to **gain** electrons to form negative ions, or share electrons. Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains 1 electron to become Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8).

The fewer electrons an atom needs to lose or gain, the more easily it reacts. This is why group 1 metals and group 17 non-metals are so reactive.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Writing a configuration

Write the electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16) and state its group and period.

1. Sulfur has 16 electrons.
2. Shell 1 takes 2 (14 left). Shell 2 takes 8 (6 left). Shell 3 takes the last 6.
3. Configuration: **2, 8, 6**.
4. Three shells are used, so it is in **period 3**. It has 6 valence electrons, so it is in **group 16** (6 + 10).

### Example 2: Configuration of an ion

Write the electron configuration of the magnesium ion, Mg²⁺.

1. A magnesium atom (Z = 12) has the configuration 2, 8, 2.
2. The 2+ charge means it has lost 2 electrons. These come from the outer shell.
3. Mg²⁺ has 10 electrons: **2, 8**.

This is the same configuration as neon. Mg²⁺ and Ne are said to be **isoelectronic** (they have the same electron arrangement).

### Example 3: Identifying an element

An element has 4 occupied shells and 2 valence electrons. Identify it.

1. Four shells means period 4.
2. Two valence electrons means group 2.
3. The configuration must be 2, 8, 8, 2, which is 20 electrons, so the element is **calcium**.

## Common mistakes

- Putting 8 electrons in the first shell. Shell 1 holds a maximum of **2**.
- Writing potassium as 2, 8, 9. For the first 20 elements, the third shell holds 8 before the fourth shell starts, so potassium is **2, 8, 8, 1**.
- Removing electrons from the inner shell when forming a positive ion. Electrons are always lost from the **outer** shell first.
- Forgetting to change the electron count for ions. Count the electrons in the ion, not in the neutral atom.
- Thinking helium belongs in group 2 because it has 2 electrons. Helium has a full shell, so it behaves like a noble gas.

## Exam tips

- Show the configuration as numbers separated by commas, and check that they add up to the number of electrons.
- When explaining reactivity, always mention valence electrons and the drive to reach a full outer shell. Saying an atom 'wants' electrons will not earn the mark on its own.
- In VCE Unit 1 you will extend this to subshells (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ …). The shell totals you learn now will still be correct, so learn them well.

## Tips to remember

- **A made-up rhyme: "Two, then eight, then eight, then two – the first twenty elements fill right through."** Shell 1 holds 2, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 holds 8, then shell 4 starts.
- **Rows = rings, columns = count.** The period number tells you how many shells are used. The group tells you how many valence electrons there are (groups 13–18: subtract 10).
- **Quick self-check:** the numbers in a configuration must add up to the atomic number. Sulfur, 2 + 8 + 6 = 16 ✓.
- **Peel ions like an onion, from the outside.** Electrons are lost from the outer shell first, so Mg (2, 8, 2) becomes Mg²⁺ (2, 8).
- **Few to lose, many to gain.** Atoms with 1–3 valence electrons (metals) lose them. Atoms with 5–7 (non-metals) gain or share electrons to reach a full outer shell.
- **Helium is the odd one out.** It has 2 electrons but sits in group 18, because its only shell is already full.

## Key terms

- **Shell (energy level)** — a region around the nucleus where electrons of similar energy are found.
- **Electron configuration** — the arrangement of electrons in the shells of an atom or ion, such as 2, 8, 1.
- **Shell diagram** — a drawing showing electrons as dots or crosses on circles around the nucleus.
- **Valence shell** — the outermost occupied shell of an atom.
- **Valence electrons** — the electrons in the valence shell; they are involved in chemical reactions.
- **Octet rule** — atoms tend to react to gain a full outer shell of 8 electrons (2 for the first shell).
- **Isoelectronic** — having the same electron configuration.

## Summary

- Electrons fill shells from the inside out; for the first 20 elements the shells hold 2, 8, 8 and 2.
- The period number equals the number of occupied shells.
- The number of valence electrons tells you the group (1 and 2, or 13 to 18 minus 10).
- Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.
- Full outer shells are stable; metals lose valence electrons and non-metals gain or share them to reach a full outer shell.
- Atoms that need to lose or gain fewer electrons are generally more reactive.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of electrons the first shell can hold?
questions.explanation: The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons, which is why helium (2) has a full shell. 8 is the maximum for the second shell and is a common mix-up.

questions.prompt: What is the electron configuration of potassium (Z = 19)?
questions.explanation: Fill shells 2, 8, 8, then the last electron goes into shell 4: 2, 8, 8, 1. Option A is tempting, but for the first 20 elements the third shell holds 8 before the fourth shell starts filling.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why lithium, sodium and potassium have similar chemical properties?

options.A: They each have one valence electron
options.B: They have the same number of shells
options.C: They have the same number of protons
options.D: They each have a full outer shell

questions.explanation: All group 1 elements have 1 valence electron, and valence electrons decide how an atom reacts. Option B is wrong: they are in different periods (2, 3 and 4), so they have different numbers of shells.

questions.prompt: Why are noble gases such as neon very unreactive?

options.B: They are gases at room temperature

questions.explanation: A full outer shell is a very stable arrangement, so there is no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons. Option B is tempting, but many reactive elements, such as fluorine and chlorine, are also gases.

questions.prompt: Which of these explains why fluorine (2, 7) forms the ion F⁻?

options.A: It loses 7 electrons to empty its outer shell
options.B: It gains 1 electron to fill its outer shell
options.C: It gains 1 proton to become stable
options.D: It shares 1 electron with another fluorine ion

questions.explanation: Gaining 1 electron gives fluorine the configuration 2, 8 (like neon) and a 1− charge. Option A would also give a full shell but losing 7 electrons takes far more energy than gaining 1, and it would form F⁷⁺, not F⁻. Protons never change in a chemical reaction.

questions.prompt: An element has the electron configuration 2, 8, 5. In which group and period is it found?
questions.explanation: It has 3 occupied shells, so it is in period 3, and 5 valence electrons, so it is in group 15 (5 + 10). This is phosphorus. Option A is tempting because it uses the old numbering, but the modern periodic table numbers this group 15.

questions.prompt: What is the electron configuration of the aluminium ion, Al³⁺ (Z = 13)?
questions.explanation: Aluminium atom is 2, 8, 3. It loses its 3 outer electrons to form Al³⁺, leaving 10 electrons: 2, 8. Option B is the neutral atom, and option C comes from adding 3 electrons instead of removing them.

questions.prompt: Which pair of particles are isoelectronic (have the same electron configuration)?
questions.explanation: Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons (2, 8, 8), the same as argon. Option B is tempting, but a neutral chlorine atom has only 17 electrons (2, 8, 7). K⁺ has 18 electrons while calcium has 20, so D is wrong.
